newsitem.title: UK: Irish minister condemns suspected IRA attack.
newsitem.headline: Irish minister condemns suspected IRA attack.

text.p: Ireland's new defence minister David Andrews on Friday condemned a grenade attack on Northern Ireland police and called on IRA guerrillas to back peace moves unveiled by British Prime Minister Tony Blair.

The ambush, described by a British official as "discouraging" after Blair's initiative on Wednesday, occurred as London wrestled with another testing problem in its volatile province -- a tension-laden "marching season" by Protestants.
Britain's Northern Ireland minister, Mo Mowlam, brought Protestant parade organisers and Roman Catholic objectors under one roof and shuttled between them while they remained in separate rooms.

She was trying for a compromise on the most hotly disputed pro-British parade at Portadown on July 6 and said she would "leave no stone unturned" to prevent a repeat of sectarian clashes that swept the province last year.

Andrews, appointed by Prime Minister Bertie Ahern who succeeded John Bruton on Thursday, said the overnight attack was outrageous. No group claimed it but British sources said the grenade was a type used before by the Irish Republican Army.

"Any attack...on the RUC or any other forces is quite an outrage -- by whatever side -- and I roundly condemn that attack," Andrews told BBC radio in an interview. He also condemned last week's murder of two Royal Ulster Constabulary police officers who were shot as they patrolled in the town of Lurgan.
"It's just not acceptable. I think that we should now get into the talks as quickly as possible based on the Blair formula."
Security sources said guerrillas fired a foreign-manufactured RPG-7 grenade at a Landrover patrolling a sectarian flashpoint zone in north Belfast. It missed and hit a wall. No-one was hurt.

The sources said it was the first time that the armour-piercing projectile was used against British forces since the IRA, waging a campaign for 28 years to end British rule in Northern Ireland and merge it into an all-Ireland state, broke a 17-month ceasefire last year.
"It was certainly used pre-ceasefire. Again we look towards republican terrorist groupings who have used that weapon in the past," police chief inspector Bob Gargin said at the scene.

Blair, in a statement to parliament on Wednesday, held out the prospect of a political settlement in Northern Ireland by next May when he outlined an Anglo-Irish strategy for taking guerrilla weaponry out of the Northern Ireland arena.
He said that three days before the Lurgan shootings, Britain had told Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, that it could enter talks six weeks after an unequivocal end to guerrilla violence.

"It appears not only to be the best offer, it is the only offer. In that regard I think they should listen to it, study it carefully and at the end of the day they include themselves (in all-party talks) by accepting it..." Andrews said.
Applauding Mowlam's bid for compromise at "proximity talks" at her official residence in Hillsborough Castle, near Belfast, Andrews hoped the rival groups would respond positively.
The talks, which officials said might continue on Saturday, were held to try and defuse rising anxiety that trouble at Portadown could ignite violence elsewhere, like last year.

Leaders of the Orange Order, a brotherhood that holds annual parades of pro-British allegiance, refuse to have face-to-face talks with Catholics whose homes are on the march route. The Catholics say such marches are inflammatory and should be confined to Protestant zones.
The marching season climaxes on July 12 when tens of thousands of Protestants mark the 1690 "Battle of the Boyne" victory by King William of Orange over the Catholic King James and his Irish forces.
If no compromise is reached over the Portadown parade, Mowlam and the police may be forced to ban it or a rival "street festival" that the Catholics plan to stage in its path.
